deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The page traces one ray through a thick biconvex lens, with one internal reflection, and uses an observed angle to fix the refractive index n. The ray starts at the axis point O (origin '0') with slope delta = -0°17'45". It refracts into the first surface (vertex at d = 108.60, radius r = 13.302, centre M at d+r = 121.902). It reflects at the second surface (vertex at d+q = 108.870, q = 0.270 the thickness, radius r' = 33.461, centre M' = d+q-r' = 75.409). It refracts out through the first surface again and reaches a point D on the same side as O, at distance D = 128.23 from O and angle gamma from the negative axis. The observed value is gamma = 9°18'51". The trial index is mu = n = 1.5310 (log n = 0.1849752). The value 'r'...1.5245389' is log r'. All arithmetic is in 7-place logarithms; 'n' after a log marks a negative number.

FORMULAS (left column), as I read them. Angles of the ray with the axis are signed. Distances are measured from the sphere centres.
1. Triangle O-P-M: sin a = ((d+r)/r) sin delta. Here a is the angle of incidence at the first surface.
2. Snell's law: sin a' = sin a / n.
3. Slope of the refracted ray: alpha = a - a' - delta.
4. The refracted ray meets the axis at distance A = r sin a' / sin alpha from M.
5. Distance of that axis point from M' is r + r' + A - q. Hence the incidence angle b at the back surface satisfies sin b = ((r+r'+A-q)/r') sin alpha.
6. Reflection: the new slope is b' = 2b - alpha.
7. The reflected ray meets the axis at B = r' sin b / sin b' from M'.
8. Its distance from M is r + r' - B - q. So the incidence angle m at the first surface (from inside) is sin m = ((r+r'-B-q)/r) sin b'.
9. Exit refraction: sin m' = n sin m.
10. Exit slope: u = m' + b' - m.
11. Axis crossing of the emergent ray: C = r sin m' / sin u, measured from M.
12. The emergent ray, through the axis point x = d + r - C with slope u, must pass through D = (-D cos gamma, D sin gamma). This gives 0 = (d+r + D cos gamma - C) tan u - D sin gamma. Gauss simplifies it by the sine rule in triangle O-X-D to sin(gamma - u) = ((d+r-C)/D) sin u.

NUMERICS (with n = 1.5310).
- log(d+r) = 2.0860108 and log r = 1.1239169, so log((d+r)/r) = 0.9620939. log sin delta = 7.7129225n.
- log sin a = 8.6750164n, so a = -2°42'43.459".
- log sin a' = 8.4900412n, so a' = -1°46'15.812".
- alpha = -0°38'42.647".
- log r sin a' = 9.6139581n and log sin alpha = 8.0515489n, so A = 36.509781.
- r + r' - q = 46.493. log(A+r+r'-q) = 1.9190927 and log(sin alpha / r') = 6.5270100n, so log sin b = 8.4461027n and b = -1°36'2.147".
- b' = -2°33'21.647".
- log r' sin b = 9.9706416n and log sin b' = 8.6492964n, so B = 20.957778.
- r + r' - q - B = 25.535222 (log 1.4071397). log sin b'/r = 7.5253795n, so log sin m = 8.9325192n and m = -4°54'39.755".
- log sin m' = 9.1174944n, so m' = -7°31'52.581".
- u = -5°10'34.473".
- log r sin m' = 0.2414113n and log sin u = 8.9553011n, so C = 19.324587.
- d + r - C = 102.577413 (log 2.0110518). Adding log sin u gives 0.9663529n. Subtracting log D = 2.1079896 gives log sin(gamma - u) = 8.8583633n.
- So gamma - u = -4°8'19.309" and gamma = u + (gamma - u) = -9°18'53.782" in magnitude.
- The required value ('s.s.' = soll sein) is 9°18'51".
- A first attempt (8.8585428, gamma - u = -4°8'28.349", gamma = 9°19'13.323") is struck out.

RESULTING POINT LIST ('Coordinaten der Hauptpunkte'). These are the salient points of the traced ray, not Gauss's cardinal points.
- D = -126.539388 + 20.7537420 i. Check: |D| = 128.23 and arg = 180° - 9°18'51".
- Surface hits P, P', P'' = 108.611... with small imaginary parts; these come from the next page's complex-coordinate trace. P'' (y = -0.5607966) is actually the first hit, since y = x tan delta.
- Axis points: A = d + r + A = 158.411781; B = M' + B = 96.366778; M = 121.902; M' = 75.409. C is listed as 19.324587, i.e. as the distance from M rather than the coordinate 102.577.

TOP BLOCK ('Schärfer ist'). Gauss re-solves with a corrected index to reproduce the observed gamma. He takes n = 1.5309377 (log 0.1849575). This gives a' = -1°46'16.072", m = -4°54'39.495", m' = -7°31'51.069", u = -5°10'32.961". The next page refines this to n = 1.5309363.

SUMMARY. The page determines the refractive index of a lens from the measured direction of a ray that has been internally reflected once (a 'ghost'/reflex image). It is done by exact trigonometric ray tracing followed by a correction of n.
errors: No genuine arithmetic errors found; every log sum and angle combination I rechecked is consistent to about 1e-7 in the logarithm (about 0.1").
The struck-out first evaluation (log sin(gamma-u) = 8.8585428, gamma = 9°19'13.323") was wrong. Gauss replaced it himself with 8.8583633n and gamma = 9°18'53.782".
The overwritten digits of log sin u must read 8.9553011n, not 8.9553041n. Only 8.9553011 reproduces both C = 19.324587 and 0.9663529n; direct computation of sin(5°10'34.473") also gives 8.9553010.

Labelling inconsistency, not a calculation error: A and B are given as absolute axis coordinates (158.41, 96.37), but C is given as the distance from M (19.3246). The absolute coordinate of C would be 102.577.
Labels P/P'' appear reversed with respect to the order of travel. P'' = 108.611829 - 0.5607966i lies on the line y = x tan delta and is the entry point.
Signs are handled loosely: gamma comes out as -9°18'53.782" in the angle convention but is compared with +9°18'51". This is a convention matter only.
The trial n = 1.5310 gives gamma about 2.8" too large, which motivates the corrected n = 1.5309377.

results.what: Exact trigonometric (meridional) ray trace through a thick lens with refraction, internal reflection at the rear surface and re-refraction, via the sine rule in centre-based triangles
results.modern_name: Exact meridional ray tracing (sine-rule / 'trigonometric ray trace')
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice in 18th–19th c. optics (e.g. Euler, Seidel, Steinheil); formalised in later lens-design texts

results.what: Determination of the refractive index of a lens from the observed direction of a once-internally-reflected ray (reflex/ghost image), by iterating n to match the measured angle gamma
results.modern_name: Refractive index determination from catadioptric (reflex) images of a lens; inverse ray-trace fitting
results.usually_credited_to: unsure; Gauss is known to have worked on lens constants around his Dioptrische Untersuchungen (1840)

results.what: Simplified closure condition sin(gamma-u) = ((d+r-C)/D) sin u for a ray through a given off-axis point
results.modern_name: Sine rule in the triangle object point – axis crossing – image point

deep.surprise_reason: This is careful but routine numerical ray tracing with logarithms, used to calibrate the refractive index of a specific lens from an internal-reflection observation. It is interesting as evidence of Gauss's practical lens measurements, but it contains no new theory.
